claims.text: Single-phase HEAs can exhibit an exceptional combination of strength and ductility under dynamic loading.
The strength–ductility combination is primarily caused by enhanced dislocation entanglement.
Severe lattice distortion induces enhanced dislocation entanglement in HEAs.
Enhanced dislocation entanglement delays dynamic recovery.
Delayed dynamic recovery gives the HEA a higher strain-hardening rate than simpler alloys.
The HEA specimens should have a homogeneous, single-phase FCC structure, controlled grain size, and minimal second phases.
The controlled comparison should use a compositionally simpler single-phase FCC alloy with microstructural features similar to those of the HEA.
Dynamic recovery mechanisms are active at the proposed test temperatures below 600 °C.
High configurational complexity in HEAs creates significant lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion promotes denser and more stable dislocation networks during plastic deformation.
The proposed mechanism increases strain-rate sensitivity in the HEA relative to a simpler alloy.
The proposed mechanism produces a higher yield stress under dynamic loading than in the simpler baseline alloy.
Relative to the baseline FCC alloy, the HEA will exhibit a higher yield stress.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA will exhibit a steeper increase in strain-hardening rate as strain rate increases.
The deformed HEA will contain a higher density of dislocation tangles and less evidence of recovery than the baseline alloy.
The hypothesis should hold from quasi-static through intermediate dynamic strain rates, below 600 °C, and only in a homogeneous single-phase state.
Differences in stacking-fault energy may cause quantitative variation in strain-rate sensitivity and yield stress.
Failure to observe higher strength and hardening together with greater dislocation entanglement, or observation of similar recovery in both alloys, would falsify the hypothesis.
